content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the formation of esters from alcohols and carboxylic acids
Describe the properties and uses of esters

are organic compounds formed from the reaction of alcohols with carboxylic acids. They are responsible for many pleasant fruity smells and flavours, and are used in perfumes, food flavourings, and as solvents.
Products of reaction between alcohol and carboxylic acid
[DIAGRAM: Structure of ester link showing -COO- arrangement with R groups]
R comes from the carboxylic acid
Ethanoic acid + Ethanol ⇌ Ethyl ethanoate + Water
Less soluble in water than alcohols
Why lower boiling points than acids?
Esters cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other
The -OH group is no longer present
Only van der Waals forces between molecules
Esters can be broken down by water:
This is the reverse of esterification.
Ethyl ethanoate + Sodium hydroxide → Sodium ethanoate + Ethanol
Write the equation for the formation of methyl propanoate.
Identify the components from the name:
Propanoic acid + Methanol ⇌ Methyl propanoate + Water
Name the ester formed when butanol reacts with ethanoic acid.

Describe how you could make a sample of ethyl ethanoate in the laboratory.
Mix ethanol and ethanoic acid in a flask
Add a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst)
Heat the mixture under reflux for 15-20 minutes
Neutralise the acid by adding sodium carbonate solution
The ester has a fruity smell
Naming esters in the wrong order
Alcohol part first, then acid part (ethyl ethanoate, not ethanoate ethyl)
Thinking esters are acids because they come from acids
Esters are neutral; they don't have a free -COOH group
Concentrated sulfuric acid is needed as a catalyst
